**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Hardware expansion versus utilisation improvement for our inference workloads

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own before committing to any new purchases. We should treat a purchase as likely but not inevitable: if utilisation work delivers the headroom we expect, we defer spending by at least two quarters; if it stalls, we will have better data and a stronger case for exactly the right purchase. This is not an argument against buying hardware — it is an argument about sequencing.

**The situation**

Our four on-premise A100 nodes currently run at roughly 35–40% average utilisation, but our p99 latency during peak hours is worse than our SLO, and we have turned away two internal teams who wanted to run batch jobs on our spare capacity. That combination — idle capacity on average, scarcity at peak — is the classic signature of a scheduling problem, not a capacity problem. It is also the pattern that most often triggers premature hardware purchases.

**Cost**

The capital case for new hardware is straightforward on its face. A fifth node costs approximately the same as one engineer-year, plus power, cooling, and rack space, and it would immediately relieve peak pressure. But that framing understates the true cost. A new node does not fix the underlying mismatch between when work arrives and when capacity is free; it simply moves the utilisation curve. If our peak-to-average ratio stays where it is, we will be back in the same position within a year, having spent capital to buy a temporary reprieve. By contrast, the utilisation work — better queueing, batch-job deferral to off-peak windows, model co-location, and possibly a modest caching layer — costs perhaps two engineer-months and produces improvements that compound across every node we own, including any we buy later.

**Latency**

The latency argument for buying is real: dedicated capacity means predictable tail latency, and no amount of clever scheduling fully eliminates contention. But our latency problem is concentrated in a narrow window, and our own traces suggest that most p99 violations come from batch jobs colliding with interactive traffic, not from raw capacity shortage. Priority-aware scheduling and time-shifting batch work would address the dominant cause directly. If, after that, interactive latency still breaches SLO at moderate load, that would be strong evidence that we genuinely need more silicon — and we would then know it with confidence rather than suspicion.

**Reliability**

Here the two options pull in opposite directions, and we should be honest about it. More hardware improves fault tolerance: with five nodes, losing one costs 20% of capacity; today, losing one of four costs 25%, and a second failure is catastrophic. Better utilisation, done carelessly, can push us toward running hotter with less slack, which is a reliability regression dressed up as efficiency. Our mitigation is to treat headroom as a deliberate design parameter: we will target sustained utilisation of no more than 60% and keep a defined failure envelope, so that efficiency gains come from scheduling intelligence rather than from eating our safety margin.

**Opportunity cost**

The scarcest resource here is not money but engineer attention. Every week spent on scheduler work is a week not spent on product features. However, the scheduler improvements we propose are durable infrastructure that pays out continuously, whereas a purchase is a one-time fix that decays as demand grows. There is also an opportunity cost on the other side: capital spent on a node now is capital unavailable for the larger refresh we will likely need within eighteen months, when newer accelerators may offer materially better price-performance. Buying today at today's prices, for capacity we can largely schedule our way out of, locks us into a weaker position for that future decision.

**Reversibility**

This is the decisive factor for me. Utilisation work is highly reversible and information-rich: every experiment teaches us something about our real demand shape, and nothing is stranded if we change course. A hardware purchase is largely irreversible — depreciating, power-hungry, and hard to resell at value — and it commits us to today's assumptions about workload growth. When one path generates information and the other consumes it, take the first.

**Uncertainty**

I want to flag two genuine unknowns. First, our utilisation numbers come from coarse instrumentation; if true idle capacity is lower than we believe, the case for buying strengthens considerably, and we should instrument properly in the first two weeks. Second, if the incoming demand from the two interested teams materialises at full scale, our headroom may be smaller than it looks, and purchase becomes the right call sooner.

**Proposed next step:** a six-week utilisation sprint with explicit success criteria agreed in advance, after which we revisit the purchase decision with real data in hand.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Hardware expansion versus utilisation improvement for our local inference fleet

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own, and defer any purchase decision until we have real utilisation data in hand. This is not a verdict that we have enough capacity — it may well turn out that we don't — but right now we are making the buy-versus-optimize call with almost no evidence, and the asymmetry of the two options strongly favours gathering that evidence first.

**Where we stand**

Our current fleet runs at roughly 25–30% utilisation by our own rough accounting, and that figure deserves scrutiny before anyone treats it as gospel. It is measured crudely, it varies enormously by time of day, and some of the "idle" capacity is idle for good reasons: it is reserved for batch jobs, held back for failover, or sits on machines whose drivers and firmware are two releases behind. Still, even discounting generously, the pattern is familiar. When a team hits a queue, the instinct is to ask for more hardware, and the honest question is whether the queue is a capacity problem or a scheduling problem. In our case, the long tail of jobs that sit waiting while other machines run near-empty suggests the latter, at least in part.

**Cost**

The cost picture is lopsided. A meaningful hardware expansion — enough GPUs to actually move the needle on peak demand, plus the networking, power, and rack space that come with them — is a six-figure commitment with a lead time measured in months. Improving utilisation is mostly an investment of engineering time: better job scheduling, a proper queueing layer, batching small inference requests, and quantising the models that can tolerate it. We estimate two to three engineers for a quarter. That is real money, but it is money we are choosing how to spend, and it produces capability — scheduling infrastructure, telemetry, batching — that we will want regardless of what we eventually buy. Hardware, by contrast, is a bet that our demand curve looks next year the way it looked last month.

**Latency**

Latency is the strongest argument on the buy side, and we should be honest about it. If interactive workloads are queueing behind batch jobs, better scheduling will help, but only up to a point; there is a floor below which no amount of clever queueing substitutes for idle silicon. If our p95 latency targets are currently being missed because of contention, and utilisation work cannot close that gap, then buying becomes defensible sooner. The right move is to instrument this properly: separate interactive from batch traffic, measure what contention actually costs us, and let that number drive the decision. Right now our latency complaints are anecdotal, and anecdotes are a poor basis for capital expenditure.

**Reliability**

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy, and if a single node failure currently degrades service, that is a genuine argument for expansion. But it also means more failure surface, more firmware to maintain, and more of the operational toil that a team our size already feels. Better utilisation, done carelessly, makes reliability worse — a fleet running at 80% has no headroom to absorb a node loss. Any utilisation push must therefore build in explicit headroom targets, and we should treat "we can lose a node and still meet SLOs" as a hard constraint, not an aspiration.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The opportunity cost of buying is the clearest of all: the engineers and budget spent on hardware are unavailable for the product work that actually generates the demand we're worried about. The opportunity cost of optimising is smaller and, crucially, the work is reversible in its benefits — scheduling and telemetry infrastructure pays off whether or not we later buy more machines. Buying hardware is largely irreversible; GPUs depreciate quickly, and if demand shifts, we own expensive heaters. Optimisation, even if it fails to fully close the gap, leaves us better informed and better instrumented for the purchase decision we may eventually need to make.

**Uncertainty**

The largest unknown is our own demand trajectory. If a major launch or a new customer lands next quarter, the calculus changes overnight, and we should not pretend otherwise. This memo should be revisited the moment demand forecasts shift materially.

**Decision requested**

Approve one quarter of focused utilisation work with a defined exit criterion: if p95 latency for interactive workloads still misses target at 70% effective fleet utilisation, we bring a hardware purchase proposal to this group with real numbers behind it.
